papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. papers.title: CoSafe: Cooperative Runtime Safety Assurance for Mixed-Traffic Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of autonomous driving systems (ADSes), real-world roads are evolving into mixed-traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other traffic participants (e.g., human-driven vehicles (HDVs), cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact with each other. However, current ADSes still incur various safety violations in mixed traffic scenarios, raising a strong demand for runtime safety assurance frameworks that can continuously monitor hazards and prevent potential violations. Existing ego-centric assurance approaches are insufficient for mixed traffic, where violations often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles and cannot be reliably resolved through independent takeover. To bridge this gap, we propose CoSafe, a modular and ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety assurance framework for mixed-traffic autonomous driving to extend runtime safety assurance from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention. CoSafe leverages vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to enable roadside units (RSUs) to monitor scene-level hazards and jointly mitigate hazards involving multiple vehicles. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and our evaluation on the InterDrive benchmark demonstrates that CoSafe improves the driving score of AVs by 70.03% on average, reduces safety violations by 87.80%, and accurately identifies unsafe AVs with an F3 score of 0.930, while satisfying real-time constraints.

papers.title: ReactWorld: Structuring Interaction Responses for Embodied Video Generation
papers.abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.

papers.title: Fluidic Body: Swarm Robots as a Fluid Extension of the Hand
papers.abstract: Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human--computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with. For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm's behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective's behavior as each task demands. We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm's behavior to each task by changing the fluid's properties through simple hand movements. When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects. We evaluated the controller's performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants). These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.

papers.title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
papers.abstract: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

papers.title: WayPOP: A Panoramic Open-Set Panoptic Tracking Benchmark
papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Information-Theoretic Decoder Evaluation Under Latent Intent
papers.abstract: A central challenge in assistive brain-to-robot control is decoding a user's latent intent from complex and noisy brain signals. Prior approaches evaluate decoders as single-trial classifiers with accuracy-based metrics, but this neglects the inherently sequential nature of assistive control. Since a planner must integrate intermittent, noisy decoder outputs over time, single-step accuracy can only be a proxy when predicting downstream task performance. We formalize brain-to-robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), and prove that there is a sharp phase transition: regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon as long as pairs of goals are all decoder-distinguishable, but grows linearly otherwise. We show that a single channel statistic, the worst-pair Chernoff information $\Gamma_{\min}$ sets this boundary. Then, we derive a closed-form regret predictor $U_{\mathrm{id}}(C)$, that can be computed from any confusion matrix in $O(K^2)$ time. Across two domains spanning orthogonal information channels, we show that $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy can explain. We then highlight a pathological accuracy trap, in which two decoders have identical validation accuracy 35.1% on real EEG data (BNCI2014001 subject 5) but result in a difference of $9.6\times$ in held-out regret, which $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts. Same-signal control confirms $U_{\mathrm{id}}$'s advantage with decoders that span independent feature channels. Ultimately, our work provides a drop-in diagnostic to evaluate and select sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control.

papers.title: Representations of 3D Rotations: Mathematical Foundations and Comparative Analysis
papers.abstract: Rotation representations are foundational in fields such as computer graphics, robotics, and machine learning, where precise and efficient modeling of 3D orientations is critical. This paper comprehensively investigates diverse representations of the special orthogonal group $SO(3)$, such as Euler angles, axis-angle vectors, quaternions, rotation matrices, exponential maps, and emerging continuous and probabilistic methods, evaluating their mathematical formulations, continuity, susceptibility to gimbal lock, computational efficiency, storage requirements, interpolation properties, and composition operations, while integrating detailed algebraic insights with practical applications in fields like animation, pose estimation, inertial navigation, 3D shape registration, and neural networks. Empirical evidence highlights quaternions' dominance due to their compactness and computational efficiency, while alternatives like 6D continuous representations and matrix Fisher distributions provide enhanced continuity and uncertainty modeling. Future research could explore hybrid methods and thorough large-scale evaluations to help build a solid foundation for improving rotation representation techniques.

executive_summary: Several works advance humanoid autonomy and loco-manipulation: Ctrl-F introduces a hierarchical motion–force framework that augments humanoid motion tracking with explicit 3D force commands, enabling large, sustained interaction forces and online load adaptation; in simulation and on real hardware it achieves hand- and foot-based dragging, pushing, lifting, and kicking of boxes up to 20 kg where a force-blind tracker fails. HALO generates large-scale paired vision–language–motion data in simulation across ~1,000 procedurally generated homes to train perceptive humanoid policies that compose skills like navigation, crouching, and box pushing, and transfers zero-shot to physical humanoids with 91% success over 360 trials in six unmapped homes. Soccerbot uses a hierarchical RL framework with a latent motion prior distilled from human soccer motion capture to learn a single skill-conditioned policy for moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking; policies transfer zero-shot to a Unitree G1, exhibiting agile, human-like soccer skills in the real world.

Data-driven and reinforcement learning methods are used to enhance control of complex robots and policies: an aSSM-based MPC framework learns an adiabatic spectral submanifold model for a soft trunk robot and achieves full-body dynamic shape regulation on hardware with ~10× accuracy over linear baselines, enabling section-wise shaping and 25+ s human-in-the-loop tennis-ball balancing where linear models and a 12 h-trained model-free RL policy fail. Another study shows that generalist robot foundation models can be improved online over diverse tasks via a carefully chosen reinforcement learning recipe, with value-based RL and training-task distribution identified as key to cross-task generalization, yielding gains on both trained and unseen tasks. A method that learns object-centric motion priors from human–object interaction data uses predicted future object states as a task-agnostic RL reward for dexterous manipulation, outperforming prior methods in success rate and generalization to novel objects across three simulated and real tasks and transferring skills across different robotic hands. A separate investigation of self-repair in code-as-policy agents for simulated manipulation finds that template-based execution feedback for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% of 252 failures within five retries versus 68.3% for resampling, with similar trends under fixed token budgets, and shows that mismatched templates can harm performance, motivating richer baselines for robot self-repair evaluations.

New benchmarks and evaluation frameworks target agentic and multimodal robotic systems: Variational Automation is proposed as a setting where robots must handle known variations in object shape and pose, and VABAR is introduced as a simulation-based benchmark with six standardized manipulation classes, difficulty tiers, metrics, and 33 skill primitives with human-authored reference solutions; baseline experiments using a Graph-as-Policy manipulation harness and Isaac Lab Arena illustrate systematic evaluation of agentic systems. For the RoboMME benchmark, a three-tier architecture combines GPT-6 Astra planning over grounded subtasks, a π₀.₅ vision-language-action policy for execution, and a Qwen3-VL-4B monitor for subtask completion detection; this design reuses high-level instructions until completion signals and achieves 79.13% episode success with 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 s per episode, surpassing the best non-oracle baseline by 34.62 percentage points and approaching a GroundSG+Oracle upper bound within 4.95 points. A controlled LeRobot-based real-robot study with visuo-tactile sensing factorizes tactile input into RGB, normal/depth, and marker-flow cues and shows that adding tactile perception raises overall success from 57.8% to 78.9%, with marker flow alone reaching 74.4% and cue-factorized encoders consistently outperforming non-factorized ones; cross-attention emerges as a lightweight yet competitive visuo-tactile fusion method.

Several motion planning and trajectory-generation advances improve performance for rigid, humanoid, and continuum systems: a contact-implicit whole-body trajectory optimization framework plans dynamic humanoid motions over smooth, uneven terrains (e.g., steps, ramps) without predefined contact sequences by modeling full dynamics and novel rigid contact constraints, with feasibility shown in simulation and on the ErgoCub humanoid. GRASP introduces gradient-informed motion retargeting without differentiable simulators by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts; GRASP-TO augments tempered SMC with these gradients, GRASP-MPC scales to long demonstrations, and experiments report 92.8% success over 1,352 bimanual OakInk2 demos and improved PPO tracking for dexterous and humanoid tasks, including successful real-hardware dexterous and whole-body motions. A trajectory generator is proposed that yields C^∞-smooth trajectories respecting kinematic limits and ensuring continuity of all derivatives (velocity through higher orders), covering null boundary conditions and addressing the higher smoothness needs of soft continuum robots; simulations and hardware experiments confirm its suitability for soft-robot motion planning. A unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots couples a global A* plus minimum-jerk path planner with a local geometry-consistent IK and Riemannian optimization layer, improving motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability over multiple baselines in simulated pipe traversal and real-world navigation/manipulation in clutter. cuRoboV2-Fast performs GPU-accelerated B-spline trajectory optimization with differentiable inverse dynamics and a TimeOpt procedure using banded Newton solves, achieving 4.4 ms mean planning time on an RTX 5090 (14.7× faster than cuRoboV2), surpassing prior GPU–CPU combinations even on a Jetson AGX Orin, and reducing a YAM pick-and-drop cycle time by 34.6% to 5.93 s.

New sensing and assistance systems target physical interaction and navigation under uncertainty: OUCH, a wrist-worn pneumatic device with stacked pouch actuators and a rigid indenter isolated by a buckling spacer, delivers controlled noxious mechanical stimuli for neurological assessment; characterization shows ~18,500 kPa estimated contact pressure at 200 kPa inflation (over 25× a commercial pressure algometer tip) while requiring less total force and localizing deformation near the surface, and preliminary tests indicate similar discomfort at ~89% lower applied force than the algometer. A planner-conditioned air–ground assistance framework for off-road navigation triggers UAV sensing only when a UGV’s MPPI rollouts degrade due to map uncertainty; by scoring rollouts against hypothesized resolved maps and requesting only the most beneficial aerial measurements, it achieves 98.9% goal completion over 180 simulations while cutting mean UAV flight time by 87.7% versus continuous greedy mapping, with field trials over ~2 km showing recovery of successful navigation in real terrain.

institution_matches.title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces OUCH, a wrist-worn pneumatic device combining stacked pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer that buckles at a set load to deliver controlled, repeatable noxious mechanical stimuli for neurological assessment. topic_matches.title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), a physics-based motion retargeting method that combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts, enabling gradient-informed Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation without requiring a differentiable simulator.
